items.title: Johnny Lala Interview, 1960-03-15
items.q: a fellow used to book, the fellow that booked us that time, Ted Weems, and his brother Art Weems was working with the Mason Dixon Orchestra, doing the same thing around that time.

ctx.x: Yeah. He don't play on that. Well, you know, Johnny, look, I don't have it in for any kind of music. As a matter of fact, I love some classical music. I don't love all classical music. I mean, everybody's got a right to pick their music. Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. The thing is that I have against the music which they call modern music, the music which is played mostly now, is that it does not have any interest. No. They don't have anything new. They think they have something new. No, they don't. But they don't have…

The only thing they got new is they all entertain, they sing and everything, you know what I mean? Yeah. I was working with an orchestra, I swear to God, let me tell you the truth up north. They were traveling around the coal mines in West Virginia, all around these places. And we were only about nine men in the band. Man, that's a good job, coal mine job, man. We'd be in this little town for three nights, man, and make $75, $100, you know what I mean? A snack. Okay. And every man named- But you didn't have a…

You mean the man, somebody knocked on his door? Santo Piccolo? Somebody knocked on his head or something. I had something with me. Mr. Tailgate you mean? Yeah. I don't know what the other call is that. I had something with me. The price of fame, huh? I was in Chicago.
